children.text: A Greco-Roman-style temple built on the Busay hills north of Cebu City by a businessman in memory of his late wife. With Cebu City and the sea visible below its grand columns and statues, it's a hugely popular photo spot, and pairs well with Tops Lookout and Sirao Flower Garden for a half-day trip.
Temple of Leah is a massive neoclassical structure standing about
10km
north of downtown Cebu, midway up the Busay hills at an elevation of several hundred meters. Cebuano businessman Teodorico Soriano Adarna began construction in

in memory of his wife of 53 years, Leah Villa Albino-Adarna, and it's often called the 'Taj Mahal of Cebu.' It was designed with 24 rooms symbolizing their married life, and is still an unfinished structure with some construction ongoing.

As you step inside, the first things you notice are the front staircase lined with massive stone columns and the golden lion statues. In the front courtyard stand a white stone fountain with water spouting from horse heads and three goddess statues, and in the central hall is a large bronze statue of Mrs. Leah. The inner rooms display collections such as books Mrs. Leah gathered on her travels, Chinese-style porcelain, and busts, and thanks to the gold ornaments and stone finishes throughout the building, photos taken from any angle look like pictures from a European trip. However, the collections have almost no explanatory signs, so it feels less like a museum and more like touring a private collector's living room.

Another appeal of Temple of Leah is the view. Standing on the temple terrace, Cebu City's high-rises, Mactan Island, and the sea beyond all fit into one frame, and on clear days you can even see the horizon toward Bohol. Go in the late afternoon and sunset light streams between the temple's columns; after dark, you can see the illuminated temple together with the city's night lights.
Teodorico was an engineer-turned-businessman who said he hoped this building would last as long as Greece's Parthenon, which has stood for nearly
2,500 years
(reported in
). The bronze statue of Mrs. Leah is
tall, and that one statue alone is reported to have cost about
. This is a memorial structure, not a tomb, and Mrs. Leah is not interred here. After its founder passed away in
November 2018
, a family dispute over control of the site followed, and in
March 2020

it was even closed for a while under a city hall order to correct business-tax issues. It is now privately run property, so operating hours and the areas open to visitors may change depending on circumstances.

It's not a historic site, but it's a place where you can feel modern Cebuano culture and the family-centered sentiment of Filipinos. It suits couples, travelers who love photography, and families with half a day free in Cebu City, and pairing it with other Busay hills attractions makes for a full afternoon itinerary.

blocks.title: Photos at the grand front staircase

children.text: The most iconic photo spot, where the wide front staircase, columns, and lion statues all fit in one frame. Shoot slightly upward from the bottom of the stairs to capture the building's grandeur.

blocks.title: See the bronze statue of Leah

children.text: The bronze statue of Mrs. Leah standing in the central hall is the very reason the temple was built. Reading the dedication plaque near the entrance changes how the building feels.

blocks.title: View of Cebu City from the terrace

children.text: From the terraces at the back and sides of the temple, you can look down over Cebu City and the Mactan Channel. The breeze is cool, making it a good spot to rest even at midday.
Between
3:30 PM and 5:30 PM
, as the sunlight comes in at an angle, long shadows fall across the gold accents and columns, giving the best photo atmosphere.

After sunset, the illuminated temple has a completely different atmosphere from daytime. However, operating hours have been adjusted recently, so check the official Facebook page before an evening visit.

blocks.title: Combine with other Busay hills sights

children.text: Tops Lookout, Sirao Flower Garden, and scenic cafes around Busay are all within
10–20 minutes
by car, making it easy to continue on a half-day driving route.

The plaza in front of the front staircase has a white stone fountain with water spouting from horse-head sculptures and three goddess statues standing at the top. After sunset, when the lights come on, the fountain and the colonnade stand out together, making for well-composed night photos. The statue of a woman holding a lamp on the terrace railing is best captured against the sunset sky.

The best-known rooms are a study-like room with bookshelves and busts, and rooms packed with Chinese-style porcelain and jars. There is almost no explanation, so browse lightly, as if looking at a private collector's room. Some rooms may be closed at certain times.

Operating hours differ by attraction, and the opening hours of Sirao Garden and the Taoist temple may change depending on the season. Asking your charter driver to put Temple of Leah in the middle of the route rather than at the end helps you prepare for shortened hours.
Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) is the closest. There are daily direct flights from Korea, and it takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila. From the airport to Temple of Leah takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
by car depending on traffic.
From Manila (Ninoy Aquino International Airport), Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and AirAsia Philippines fly nonstop to Cebu, with a flight time of about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Promotional fares start from around
one way, but vary greatly by airline and date. After arriving in Cebu, take one of the airport transfer options below into the city, then head up to the temple.
In front of the Mactan-Cebu airport terminal, MyBus shuttles run to SM City Cebu and IT Park for about
. They run every
20–30 minutes
during the day, and the last bus is around 9:40 PM. White metered taxis cost about
to the city, the airport's yellow taxis about
, and Grab about
. The ride takes
30 minutes–1 hour
depending on traffic.
This is the most practical option. From central Cebu City (IT Park, Ayala), it takes about
30–40 minutes
by Grab or taxi, about

one way. It's hard to catch a ride back near the temple, so it's better to negotiate a waiting fee with the driver and charter a round trip or a tour of several sights. A half-day charter touring multiple Busay hills spots runs about
To go cheaply, take a jeepney or taxi to around JY Square Mall (Lahug), then take a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) up the hill. Negotiate about
per person one way, and ask for a helmet, since the road is steep. There is also a jeepney route toward Busay, but it is hard for first-time visitors to work out.
For the jeepney, look for routes 04D, 04I, and 04H running between Lahug and Busay. The fare is about
; tell the driver to let you off at the entrance of the road up to the temple, then walk uphill for about
5 minutes
. Route numbers may change, so confirm with the driver or locals.
From Lahug, follow the Cebu Transcentral Highway up to Busay. The road is narrow and steep, so turn on navigation (Google Maps) and drive slowly. Parking at the temple costs about
per car. Several forks toward Sirao Garden and Tops Lookout appear on the way up, so it helps to save your destination before you arrive.
During the dry season from
December
to
May

, clear skies give the longest views across the city. Being on a hill, the temperature is 1–3°C lower than downtown and there's a breeze, making it relatively pleasant even at midday. During the rainy season,
June–November
, afternoon showers and mist often cloud the view, so a morning visit is better.
During the third week of
January

's Sinulog Festival, the Easter holidays, and the Christmas season, many local families visit, making weekend afternoons very crowded. To take photos at leisure, aim for weekday mornings or right after opening.
Cebu is hot all year, but after sunset the hilltop is cooler than downtown. Sunset falls around
throughout the year, so if you want sunset photos, it's best to arrive around
. Typhoons mainly affect the rainy season and continue through late autumn and year-end; Typhoon Odette in
December 2021
and Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) in
November 2025
caused major damage in Cebu. Right after a typhoon, hill roads may be blocked and some facilities may be closed.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is almost no accommodation around Temple of Leah, so it's common to stay in Cebu City and visit as a day trip. The closest lodging areas are IT Park and Lahug, around
30 minutes
by car, with business hotels running about
a night. In the Busay hills there are a few campsites and small lodge-style accommodations with good views, used by travelers who want to enjoy the night view for longer.

Inside the temple there's a simple cafe and snack stand. For a proper meal, use the scenic restaurants and cafes along the Busay hills road, where you can enjoy Filipino grilled dishes and home-style food like sisig and caldereta together with the city night view. Returning downtown to have dinner at a lechon shop around Lahug or at Larsian barbecue alley is also a good way to finish the day.

If you stay downtown, the Ayala and IT Park area has shopping malls and restaurants close together, making dinner and Grab bookings easy, while the resort district on Mactan Island near the airport is great for a beach getaway but takes more than
1 hour

by car to reach the temple. In the Busay hills there are scenic restaurants such as Lantaw Native Restaurant, where you can enjoy Filipino regional dishes on a terrace overlooking the city's night lights. Typical Cebu foods are Cebu lechon (whole roast pig stuffed with lemongrass and other aromatic herbs) and pusô (hanging rice, rice wrapped in palm leaves and steamed), eaten with barbecue. Cebu souvenirs such as dried mangoes are easier to buy at downtown shopping malls.
Entrance fees are often cash-only and change may be limited, so prepare
and
bills.
Operating hours were long known to be
6:00 AM to 11:00 PM
, but a notice of shortened hours was issued in
. Check the official Facebook page before visiting.
Grab is easy to catch going up, but hard to get for the trip back down. Arrange a round-trip charter or agree on a return ride in advance.
The most popular photo spots are the bottom of the front staircase, in front of the central bronze statue, and the side terrace railing. You may need to queue on weekend afternoons.
Using a tripod, drone photography, or commercial shoots (such as wedding snaps) may require separate permission or a fee, so ask at the ticket booth.
The stairs and floors are polished and slippery after rain. Wear shoes with sturdy soles.
The wind can pick up on the hilltop at dusk, so it's good to bring a light jacket.
The most accurate way to learn the operating hours is to ask the temple directly. The contact number given is 0933-1131755, and announcements can also be found on the
official Facebook page
There is almost no commentary on the interior collections and not many display rooms, so
1–2 hours
is enough for a visit. Because this is a memorial site honoring the deceased, neat attire and a quiet visit are recommended.
The colonnade has a roof, so you can briefly shelter from a passing shower. However, do not stay on the outdoor terrace on the hilltop during lightning.
The road up into the Busay hills has many steep grades and sharp curves. When riding a habal-habal, ask for a helmet and request that the driver not speed.
Some areas of the temple are still under construction, so don't cross the barrier lines.
Climbing onto or leaning against statues and decorations for photos is prohibited.
If you come down late at night, transport may no longer be running, so be sure to secure a way home.
The Busay hills are prone to landslides. During Typhoon Paeng in
October 2022
, a landslide in nearby Sitio Garahe led to the area around Temple of Leah being designated a danger zone, so postpone hill visits on days with heavy rain or typhoon warnings.
In
November 2025

, Typhoon Tino caused continuing landslide and flood damage in the mountain areas of Cebu City, and the water supply around Busay was restricted for a while. Right after heavy rain, check road conditions before you visit.
Temple of Leah is private property. Operating hours, fees, and photography rules can change without notice, so check the latest announcements.
